title: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
summary: How masked diffusion LMs like LLaDA and Mercury generate text by iteratively unmasking tokens in parallel: the masking process, the likelihood-bound loss, remasking samplers, and the speed tradeoffs.
outcomes: Explain how a masked diffusion LM's forward masking process and its exact reverse define a generative model
Compute the masked diffusion training loss for a sequence and explain why it weights by 1/t
Trace low-confidence remasking step by step and predict how many tokens each step commits
Explain why parallel unmasking breaks token dependencies and when a confidence threshold makes it safe
Compare diffusion and autoregressive LMs on passes, compute, caching, quality and reversal reasoning

lessons.title: Why generate text in any order other than left to right?

blocks.md: The GPT you built is an **autoregressive model (ARM)**: it factorizes the probability of a sequence as a product of next-token conditionals, $p_\theta(x) = \prod_i p_\theta(x^i \mid x^1, \dots, x^{i-1})$. Training is parallel thanks to teacher forcing, but generation is not. To produce 256 tokens the model must run 256 forward passes one after another, because token 257 cannot be predicted until token 256 exists.

Each of those decode passes does very little arithmetic per weight it reads: one new token per sequence goes through the whole network. With a **KV cache** (the stored keys and values of earlier tokens, so they are not recomputed) the work per pass is small, and the GPU spends most of its time moving weights from memory rather than computing. Latency is set by the number of sequential passes.

The left-to-right order has two other costs. A token, once emitted, is never revised. And the model only ever learns conditionals in one direction. The **reversal curse** (Berglund et al., 2023) is the classic symptom: a model trained on "A is B" often fails to answer "what is B?" with A.

scenes.caption: An autoregressive model emits one token per forward pass. Eight tokens need eight passes in strict order, no matter how big the GPU is.
A masked diffusion model starts from 8 mask tokens and, in each pass, predicts every masked position at once. Here 4 steps each commit 2 tokens: half as many sequential passes.
Side by side. Simplified: without a KV cache, each diffusion pass recomputes the whole sequence, so it is more work per pass. Fewer passes only wins when the GPU has spare compute.

blocks.md: **Diffusion models** take a different route, proven first on images. A fixed **forward process** gradually corrupts data with noise until nothing is left; a network learns the **reverse process** that removes noise a little at a time. Generation starts from pure noise and refines the whole sample over a chosen number of steps.

For text, the most successful noise has turned out to be the simplest: replace tokens with a special **[MASK]** token. Austin et al. (D3PM, 2021) called this an **absorbing state**, because once a token becomes [MASK] it stays masked for the rest of the forward process. Models built on it are **masked diffusion models (MDMs)**. Generation then means: start with all positions masked and repeatedly fill some in.

blocks.title: Which positions each token may attend to

scenes.caption: Your GPT uses a causal mask: row i (the query) may only see columns up to i. Position 3 cannot look at 'on' or 'mat' when it is predicted.
A mask predictor drops the causal mask. Every position sees every other position, so the masked slot at position 3 can use both 'cat' on its left and 'on' and 'mat' on its right.

blocks.caption: The generative modeling principle. LLaDA's argument: scaling, in-context learning and instruction following come from maximizing likelihood with a big Transformer, not from the left-to-right factorization itself.

blocks.md: A diffusion language model keeps the Transformer and the maximum-likelihood goal of a GPT. It changes two things: attention is bidirectional, and generation fills in many masked positions per step in any order instead of one token at the end.

A masked diffusion LM is not just BERT. BERT masks a fixed 15% of tokens and has no way to sample a whole text. A masked diffusion LM trains on every masking ratio from 0 to 1 with a loss that bounds the likelihood, which is exactly what makes generation from an all-mask sequence possible.

blocks.prompt: LLaDA can generate a 256-token answer in 64 steps. How many sequential forward passes is that, and how many tokens does each pass process if the prompt is 894 tokens?
blocks.reveal: 64 sequential passes instead of 256. But LLaDA has no KV cache, so each pass processes the full prompt plus the full answer: 894 + 256 = 1150 tokens. An autoregressive model with a cache processes those 1150 tokens about once in total. Diffusion trades **more total compute** for **fewer sequential steps**, which pays off when decoding is memory-bound.

blocks.question: Why is autoregressive decoding slow on a GPU even though the GPU can do far more arithmetic per second than one token needs?
options: Each step must wait for the previous token, and each step does little compute per byte of weights read, so the GPU idles on memory traffic
Softmax over the vocabulary is the dominant cost and cannot be parallelized
The KV cache makes every step recompute attention over all earlier tokens from scratch
Causal attention needs more FLOPs than bidirectional attention
blocks.explain: Decode is sequential (token t+1 needs token t) and memory-bound: each pass streams all weights to process one token per sequence. A KV cache avoids recomputation; it does not create it. Causal attention actually computes fewer scores than bidirectional attention.

blocks.question: What does the 'absorbing state' in masked diffusion refer to?
options: The final layer of the Transformer that absorbs all positional information
The [MASK] token: once the forward process masks a token, it stays masked
The end-of-sequence token that stops generation
A Gaussian noise vector added to token embeddings
blocks.explain: In D3PM's absorbing-state process every token moves to [MASK] at some point and never leaves it. At the final time the sequence is entirely masked, which gives a simple known starting point for generation.

lessons.title: The forward process: masking as noise, and its exact reverse

blocks.md: Let $x_0$ be a clean training sequence of length $L$ and let the **time** $t$ run from 0 to 1. The forward process produces a partly masked copy $x_t$: every token is replaced by [MASK] (written M) independently with probability $t$, and kept with probability $1-t$. At $t=0$ nothing is masked; at $t=1$ everything is.

blocks.tex: q_{t|0}(x_t^i \mid x_0^i) = \begin{cases} 1 - t, & x_t^i = x_0^i \\ t, & x_t^i = \mathrm{M} \end{cases} \qquad q_{t|0}(x_t \mid x_0) = \prod_{i=1}^{L} q_{t|0}(x_t^i \mid x_0^i)
blocks.caption: LLaDA's forward process (its Eq. 7 and 8). The masking probability grows linearly in t, on the reasoning that information in text is roughly proportional to the number of tokens.

blocks.title: One sentence moving through the forward process

scenes.caption: t = 0: the clean sentence. Each token gets one uniform random number u (computed with a seeded generator); a token is masked at time t when its u is below t.
t = 0.25: tokens with u < 0.25 are masked. That is 3 of 8, while the expected count is tL = 2. The count itself is random.
t = 0.5: 'sat' (u = 0.28) joins the masks, giving 4 of 8. Reusing the same draws makes the masks nest, which is a simplification for display; each t is still marginally correct.
t = 0.75: 7 of 8 masked. Only 'today' (u = 0.89) survives. The model at this noise level sees almost no context.
t = 1: every token is masked. This all-mask sequence is the known starting point of generation, the text analogue of pure Gaussian noise for images.

blocks.md: Because each token is masked independently, the number masked is Binomial($L$, $t$). Its mean is $tL$, but for a short sequence the spread is large. This matters later: it is why LLaDA evaluates likelihoods by masking an exact count of tokens instead.

blocks.title: How many of 8 tokens get masked?

scenes.caption: t = 0.5: the most likely count is 4, but only with probability 0.273. Counts 3 to 5 together cover 0.711.
t = 0.25: centred on 2 (probability 0.311), and there is a 0.1 chance that nothing at all is masked, which gives no training signal.

blocks.md: To generate we must run time backwards. For two times $0 \le s < t \le 1$, the exact reverse of this forward process factorizes over positions too. A token that is already visible stays as it is. A masked token stays masked with probability $s/t$, and otherwise is revealed with probability $(t-s)/t$, its value drawn from $q_{0|t}$, the distribution of the clean token given what is visible.

blocks.tex: q_{s|t}(x_s^i \mid x_t) = \begin{cases} 1, & x_t^i \ne \mathrm{M},\ x_s^i = x_t^i \\ \frac{s}{t}, & x_t^i = \mathrm{M},\ x_s^i = \mathrm{M} \\ \frac{t-s}{t}\, q_{0|t}(x_s^i \mid x_t), & x_t^i = \mathrm{M},\ x_s^i \ne \mathrm{M} \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
blocks.caption: The reverse step (LLaDA Eq. 10). Everything is known in closed form except q, the prediction of the original token at a masked position. That one function is what the neural network learns.

blocks.md: There is a further simplification. The visible tokens in $x_t$ are just copies of tokens in $x_0$, and which ones survived carries no information about the hidden ones. So $q_{0|t}(x^i \mid x_t) = p_{\text{data}}(x_0^i \mid x_t^{\text{UM}})$, where $x_t^{\text{UM}}$ is the set of unmasked tokens. The time $t$ drops out, and the network does not need $t$ as an input (proved by Ou et al. and restated in LLaDA's appendix).

MDLM (Sahoo et al., 2024) builds these facts into the network as the **SUBS parameterization**: the logit of [MASK] is set to minus infinity, so the model never predicts a mask (**zero masking probabilities**), and any visible input token is copied to the output unchanged (**carry-over unmasking**). Both simplify the bound; in MDLM's LM1B ablation, carry-over unmasking is worth about 1.5 perplexity points, while zero masking makes no meaningful difference.

The forward process is fixed and trivial. The only thing to learn is a **mask predictor**: given a partly masked sequence, output a distribution over the vocabulary at every masked position. It needs no timestep input.

blocks.prompt: A reverse step goes from t = 0.5 to s = 0.25 on a sequence with 4 masked tokens. Under the exact reverse process, how many tokens do you expect to be revealed, and can a visible token change?
blocks.reveal: Each masked token stays masked with probability $s/t = 0.25/0.5 = 0.5$, so on average 2 of the 4 are revealed. Visible tokens are carried over with probability 1, so in this basic sampler a committed token never changes. That is the absorbing property running backwards.

blocks.question: Why can the mask predictor ignore the time t?
options: Because t is always 0.5 during training
Because the visible tokens are exact copies of the clean ones, so the best prediction of a hidden token depends only on what is visible, not on how much noise was applied
Because the Transformer's positional encoding already contains t
It cannot; LLaDA concatenates t to every token embedding
blocks.explain: The posterior of a masked token given x_t equals the data conditional given the unmasked tokens, which is time-invariant. The number of visible tokens already reflects the noise level, so feeding t adds nothing. MDLM also reports similar perplexity with and without time conditioning.

blocks.question: In a reverse step from t to s, a masked position stays masked with probability s/t. What happens when s = 0?
options: Every masked position is revealed in this step
Nothing is revealed, because s/t = 0 means no change
Half of the masked positions are revealed
The visible tokens are remasked
blocks.explain: With s = 0 the probability of staying masked is 0/t = 0, so every remaining mask must be filled. The last step of any schedule ends at s = 0 and finishes the sequence.

lessons.title: Training: a weighted average of masked-LM losses

blocks.md: The mask predictor is a Transformer like your GPT, with RMSNorm, SwiGLU and RoPE in LLaDA's case, but with **no causal mask**. It takes a partly masked sequence and outputs logits at every position. Training is one line different from BERT, and that line is what turns a fill-in-the-blank model into a generative model.

blocks.title: One training step of a masked diffusion LM

nodes.label:
mask each token
with prob. t

scenes.caption: Draw a noise level t uniformly, then mask each token of the clean sequence independently with probability t.
The bidirectional Transformer sees x_t (masked and visible tokens together) and predicts a token distribution at every position in one pass.
Only masked positions are scored against the clean tokens, and the sum is divided by t L. Visible positions contribute nothing; the model would just copy them.

blocks.caption: LLaDA's pre-training loss (Eq. 3). In practice one t is drawn per sequence and the sum is also divided by L. The indicator restricts the loss to masked tokens.

blocks.title: Worked example: the loss for one sequence at t = 0.5

scenes.caption: The sentence from lesson 2 at t = 0.5: positions 2, 3, 4 and 8 are masked. Those four are the only positions that will be scored.
The model's probability for the correct token at each masked slot (toy values chosen for illustration). '.' at the end is easy; 'cat' has many plausible alternatives.
Negative log-probabilities, computed: 1.204 + 0.799 + 0.511 + 0.105 = 2.619. Visible positions add zero.
Divide by t L = 0.5 x 8 = 4: the loss is 2.619 / 4 = 0.655. Four masked tokens, so this is the average per masked token.

blocks.md: Now take the same sentence at t = 0.25, where 3 tokens are masked ('cat', 'on', '.'). With more context the model is more confident: say probabilities 0.40, 0.70 and 0.95. The summed loss is only 1.324, but the divisor is also smaller, t L = 2, so the loss is 0.662. The $1/t$ factor rescales each noise level by the number of tokens it is expected to mask, $tL$.

scenes.caption: On average a fraction t of tokens is masked, so the raw sum of masked losses scales with t.
Weighting by 1/t blows up at small t, where only a few tokens are masked.
Their product is 1 at every t: each noise level gets equal say in the objective, measured per masked token. This weighting is what makes the loss a bound on likelihood.

blocks.md: This weighting is not a heuristic. Shi et al., Sahoo et al. (MDLM) and Ou et al. proved that $\mathcal{L}(\theta)$ is an **upper bound on the negative log-likelihood**, $-\mathbb{E}\log p_\theta(x_0) \le \mathcal{L}(\theta)$. MDLM describes it as a weighted average of masked-language-modeling losses. MaskGIT used a similar objective without the $1/t$ factor, which loses the link to maximum likelihood; BERT uses a single fixed ratio and so never learns the nearly-all-masked regime that generation starts from.

blocks.code:
def mdm_loss(model, x0, mask_id):
    # x0: (B, L) token ids
    B, L = x0.shape
    t = torch.rand(B, 1).clamp_min(1e-3)         # one noise level per sequence
    masked = torch.rand(B, L) < t                # mask each token with prob t
    xt = torch.where(masked, mask_id, x0)
    logits = model(xt)                           # bidirectional, no t input
    ce = F.cross_entropy(logits.transpose(1, 2), x0, reduction='none')  # (B, L)
    return ((ce * masked) / t).sum() / (B * L)   # only masked tokens, weight 1/t
blocks.caption: A minimal PyTorch version of LLaDA's Algorithm 1 (the loss is divided by t L per sequence, then averaged over the batch).

blocks.md: **Fine-tuning** keeps the same loss. For a prompt and response pair, only response tokens are masked; the prompt stays visible. LLaDA pads short responses in a batch with end-of-sequence tokens (|EOS|) and trains on them like any token, so the model learns to end its answer by filling the tail with |EOS|.

**Evaluating likelihood** (for multiple-choice benchmarks) uses an equivalent form with lower variance: draw a count $l$ uniformly from 1 to $L$, mask exactly $l$ tokens, and weight by $L/l$. LLaDA reports that the independent-masking form needs over 1000 Monte Carlo samples (independent random maskings averaged together) for stable results while the exact-count form needs 128, because it removes the binomial spread you saw in lesson 2.

Perplexities reported for diffusion LMs are usually upper bounds (written as a less-or-equal sign in the papers), not exact values. Comparing a bound to an autoregressive model's exact perplexity slightly favours the autoregressive model.

blocks.question: Spot the bug: a colleague's loss is `(ce * masked).sum() / masked.sum()`, the plain average over masked tokens, with t still drawn uniformly. What changes?
options: Nothing; it is the same quantity
The loss now includes visible tokens

Summed over the batch and divided by the total masked count, every masked token gets equal weight, so heavily masked sequences dominate; the 1/t factor is lost and it is no longer the likelihood bound
The model will learn to predict [MASK] tokens
blocks.explain: Over a large batch the ratio tends to E[sum of masked losses] / E[count]: the unweighted MaskGIT-style objective with no 1/t, which LLaDA notes lacks a link to maximum likelihood. The principled loss divides each sequence by t L. Dividing each sequence by its own masked count would actually be fine: with uniform t the count is uniform on 0 to L, giving the exact-count form LLaDA uses for likelihoods.

blocks.question: Why does training on t drawn from all of [0, 1] matter for generation, compared with BERT's fixed 15%?
options: Generation starts from a fully masked sequence, so the model must be good at predicting with almost no context; a fixed 15% ratio never trains that regime
Uniform t makes training cheaper per step
It lets the model use a causal mask
It removes the need for a tokenizer
blocks.explain: Sampling walks t from 1 down to 0, visiting every masking ratio. A model that only ever saw 15% masks has never learned the early, nearly empty steps, and its loss is not a likelihood bound.

lessons.title: Sampling: predict every mask, keep the confident, remask the rest

blocks.md: Generation runs the reverse process with $N$ discrete steps. Fix a response length $L$, fill it with [MASK], and step time from $t = 1$ down to 0 in increments of $1/N$. At each step from $t$ to $s = t - 1/N$, one forward pass predicts every masked position, and then a fraction $s/t$ of the newly predicted tokens is put back to [MASK] so that the expected number of masks matches the forward process at time $s$.

Which tokens get remasked? The exact reverse process says: a random subset (LLaDA's Algorithm 4, **random remasking**). LLaDA's default instead uses **low-confidence remasking** (Algorithm 5, taken from MaskGIT): it scores each prediction by its probability, keeps the most confident, and remasks the rest. After the step from t to s, floor(L(1 - s)) positions are unmasked; tokens already committed get confidence 1 and are never remasked.

scenes.caption: The prompt asks for the capital of France; the response is 8 positions, all [MASK], and we will use N = 4 steps. The response length is a hyperparameter fixed before sampling starts.
Step 1 (t = 1 to s = 0.75): one forward pass predicts all 8 positions. Keep floor(8 x (1 - 0.75)) = 2. The two |EOS| slots at the end are the most confident, so they are committed first.
Step 2 (s = 0.5): committed tokens count as confidence 1, so keep 4 in total: the two |EOS| plus position 6 (|EOS|, 0.96) and 'Paris' (0.88). Every other prediction is thrown away and remasked.
Step 3 (s = 0.25): keep 6. 'is' (0.93) and '.' (0.91) now beat 'The' (0.62), because the model can see 'Paris' and the end of the answer.
Step 4 (s = 0): keep all 8. The answer is 'The city is Paris .' and the |EOS| tokens are stripped. Four passes for eight tokens.

blocks.md: The confidences in the figure are illustrative, but the order they produce is the real behaviour LLaDA reports. Because supervised fine-tuning pads answers with |EOS|, the instruct model becomes very confident about |EOS| at the tail. Under pure diffusion this produced too many |EOS| tokens and very short answers, so for several benchmarks the authors set the confidence of |EOS| to zero during sampling.

scenes.caption: Random remasking, the exact reverse process, with 256 tokens generated in 256 steps.
Low-confidence remasking on the same model: GSM8K goes from 21.3 to 70.0. The authors liken it to the annealed (low-temperature) sampling that autoregressive models use by default.

blocks.title: A simplified LLaDA sampler

scenes.caption: The response starts as L masks after the prompt.
Step 1 runs from t = 1 to s = 0.75.
A single forward pass scores every position. Greedy argmax is LLaDA's default (temperature 0).
Keep floor(8 x 0.25) = 2 most confident positions; remask the other 6.
Step 2: t = 0.75, s = 0.5. Committed tokens are carried over with confidence 1, so they always survive the top-k.
Step 4 ends at s = 0, so n_un = 8 and every position is filled.

blocks.md: **Steps trade quality for speed.** With a 256-token answer, 256 steps reveal one token per pass; 64 steps reveal four per pass. LLaDA's paper shows quality falling as tokens per pass rise, and on GSM8K and Math its 8B base model matched LLaMA3 8B's accuracy at 1.5 and 1.8 times the throughput, without any caching.

**Semi-autoregressive (block) sampling** splits the answer into blocks, runs the diffusion steps inside one block at a time, and moves left to right across blocks. In the official `generate.py` this is the `block_length` argument (the mask token id is 126336). For LLaDA 8B Instruct, block sampling lifted GSM8K from 69.4 to 78.6 with block length 8, because it stops |EOS| from being committed at the tail too early.

A sampling step is: one forward pass over the whole sequence, a guess at every masked slot, then keep the k most confident guesses and remask the rest. The schedule fixes k per step; the confidence ranking decides the order.

blocks.question: With L = 256 and N = 32 steps, how many tokens are committed per forward pass on average, and how many passes are needed?
options: 1 token per pass, 256 passes
8 tokens per pass, 32 passes
32 tokens per pass, 8 passes
It depends on the prompt length
blocks.explain: The linear schedule spreads 256 unmaskings evenly over 32 steps: 256 / 32 = 8 per pass, 32 passes in total. That is the 8-tokens-per-pass point in LLaDA's sampling-efficiency figure.

blocks.question: LLaDA 8B Instruct, under pure diffusion sampling, gives very short answers on math benchmarks. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model was trained with a causal mask
The response length hyperparameter was set too large
Random remasking was used by default
Fine-tuning data padded with |EOS| makes tail |EOS| predictions highly confident, so low-confidence remasking commits them first
blocks.explain: Padding teaches the model that the tail is |EOS|, and low-confidence remasking commits the most confident tokens first. The fixes LLaDA used were to zero the |EOS| confidence or to sample block by block.

lessons.title: Why parallel decoding breaks, and how to make it fast

blocks.md: If one pass can fill eight masks, why not fill all 256 in one pass? Because the model outputs a separate distribution for each masked position, all computed from the same input. Sampling several positions in one step draws each from its own **marginal**, as if they were independent given what is visible. Real text is full of dependencies between neighbouring tokens.

blocks.prompt: Prompt: 'The list of poker hands that consist of two English words are: __ __'. The true answers are equally likely: 'high card', 'two pair', 'full house', 'straight flush'. If a model knows each position's marginal exactly and fills both blanks in one step, how often is the pair a real hand?
blocks.reveal: Each blank's marginal is uniform over 4 words, so the product of marginals spreads probability 1/16 over all 16 combinations. Only 4 combinations are real hands: 4 x 1/16 = 0.25. Three times in four you get nonsense like 'high house'. This example comes from Song and Zhou and is used in the Fast-dLLM paper.

blocks.title: True joint vs product of marginals for two blanks

scenes.caption: The true joint distribution: each real hand has probability 0.25 and mixed pairs have 0.
Product of marginals: each real hand gets 0.0625 and the 12 mixed pairs share 0.75. The coherent total is 0.25.
Fill one blank per step instead: after 'full' is committed, the next pass sees it and puts all its mass on 'house'. Sequential steps restore the dependency, at the cost of an extra pass.

blocks.tex: \underbrace{p(x^i \mid x_t)\, p(x^j \mid x_t)}_{\text{what parallel decoding samples}} \;\ne\; \underbrace{p(x^i \mid x_t)\, p(x^j \mid x_t, x^i)}_{\text{the true joint}}
blocks.caption: The conditional independence assumption behind parallel unmasking. The more tokens unmasked in one step, the larger the mismatch can be.

blocks.md: When is parallel decoding safe? Fast-dLLM (Wu et al., 2025) proves a clean condition. Suppose each of $n$ positions has a top token with marginal probability above $1 - \epsilon$. If $(n+1)\epsilon \le 1$, then the greedy choice from the product of marginals equals the greedy choice from the true joint, and the bound is tight. Confident tokens can be committed together; uncertain ones should wait.

blocks.title: Confidence needed to unmask n tokens at once

scenes.caption: From the Fast-dLLM theorem: committing n tokens in one step is guaranteed to match greedy sequential decoding when every one of them has confidence above 1 - 1/(n+1). Ten tokens at once need more than 10/11, about 0.909, each.

blocks.md: This motivates **confidence-aware parallel decoding**: instead of a fixed number of tokens per step, commit every masked token whose confidence exceeds a threshold, and always commit at least the single most confident one so the loop makes progress. Easy stretches (boilerplate, closing brackets, |EOS| runs) go many tokens at a time; hard stretches go one at a time.

The second obstacle is the **KV cache**. In a causal model, a token's keys and values never change once computed, so they can be stored. With bidirectional attention, every key and value depends on every other token, including masks that are about to be filled. An exact cache is impossible, so LLaDA recomputes the entire sequence on every step.

Fast-dLLM observed that keys and values barely change between adjacent steps (cosine similarity near 1) and caches them approximately. Generation proceeds block by block; the prompt and finished blocks are cached and refreshed once per block. **DualCache** also caches the all-mask suffix, so a step only recomputes the current block.

blocks.title: A simplified cost model: 894-token prompt, 256-token answer

scenes.caption: Sequential forward passes. An autoregressive model needs about 256; diffusion needs as many passes as steps.

Token positions pushed through the network, in thousands. AR: 1150 tokens once. No cache: steps x 1150, so 294k and 73.6k. DualCache with 8 blocks of 32: one full pass per block plus 7 block-only passes, about 11.0k.

blocks.title: Fast-dLLM on LLaDA Instruct, GSM8K 5-shot, 256 tokens

scenes.caption: Measured throughput on one A100 at batch size 1, as reported by Fast-dLLM. Speedups 3.2x, 2.5x and 8.1x; accuracy 79.3, 79.5, 79.2 and 78.5.

blocks.md: Diffusion decoding uses fewer sequential passes but more total compute per answer. It wins wall-clock time only when each pass is memory-bound (small batches, interactive latency). Caching and confidence thresholds exist to shrink the compute overhead without giving back the parallelism.

Do not read 'parallel generation' as 'all tokens in one step'. Quality drops quickly when many interdependent tokens are committed together; useful systems unmask a few to a few dozen tokens per pass depending on confidence.

blocks.question: You set Fast-dLLM's threshold so that, in a hard reasoning span, no masked token reaches it. What does the sampler do?
options: It commits the single most confident token, so it degrades gracefully to one token per pass
It stalls until the model becomes more confident
It commits every token in the block anyway
It restarts the block with a new random seed
blocks.explain: The threshold rule always unmasks the highest-confidence token to guarantee progress. In uncertain regions the sampler becomes sequential, which is exactly where dependencies between tokens matter most.

blocks.question: Why can a diffusion LM not use an exact KV cache the way a GPT does?
options: Its vocabulary is too large
It uses grouped-query attention
Bidirectional attention makes every position's keys and values depend on all other positions, which change whenever a mask is filled
Diffusion models have no keys or values
blocks.explain: In a causal model, later tokens never affect earlier keys and values, so caching is exact. Without the causal mask, filling any position changes every layer's activations everywhere. Fast-dLLM reuses them approximately because adjacent steps change them very little.

lessons.title: Where diffusion LMs stand: results, block diffusion, and limits

blocks.md: The idea took several steps to become competitive. D3PM (Austin et al., 2021) generalized discrete diffusion to structured transition matrices, including absorbing-state masking. SEDD (Lou et al., 2023) introduced a score-entropy loss and was competitive with GPT-2 on perplexity. MDLM (Sahoo et al., 2024) showed that a simple masked objective with good engineering narrows the gap further. LLaDA (Nie et al., 2025) scaled masked diffusion to 8B parameters trained from scratch.

blocks.title: LM1B test perplexity, ~110M models, 33B training tokens

scenes.caption: From MDLM's Table 1 (lower is better). Diffusion values are upper bounds. MDLM closed much of the gap to a retrained autoregressive baseline, but a gap remains (22.32 vs at most 27.04). The D3PM entry is a 70M model.

blocks.md: LLaDA 8B was pre-trained on 2.3 trillion tokens using 0.13 million H800 GPU hours, then fine-tuned on 4.5 million prompt and response pairs, with no reinforcement learning. Its base model is close to LLaMA3 8B Base overall, which saw about 15 trillion tokens, and is stronger on math and Chinese tasks while weaker on several general benchmarks.

blocks.title: LLaDA 8B Base vs LLaMA3 8B Base (same eval protocol)

scenes.caption: LLaMA3 8B Base, as re-evaluated by the LLaDA authors.
LLaDA 8B Base: level on MMLU and HumanEval, ahead on GSM8K and Math, behind on BBH and HellaSwag. The authors attribute part of this to differences in training data.

blocks.title: Reversal curse: completing Chinese poems (496 pairs)

scenes.caption: Forward: given a line, produce the next one. The autoregressive models are far stronger.
Reversal: produce the previous line. GPT-4o drops to 34.3 while LLaDA drops only from 51.8 to 45.6, since it was trained to predict tokens from context on both sides.

blocks.md: **Mercury** (Inception Labs, 2025) is a commercial diffusion LLM family. Its technical report describes a Transformer trained with a diffusion loss on the order of trillions of tokens and served by a proprietary engine with custom kernels and dynamic batching; the training details are not public. Independent measurements by Artificial Analysis (API endpoints, early 2025) put Mercury Coder Mini at 1109 and Small at 737 output tokens per second on H100s.

blocks.title: Coding models: API throughput and HumanEval

scenes.caption: Output tokens per second as reported in the Mercury report (measured by Artificial Analysis; for the other models, the median across API providers). Mercury Coder Mini is about 5.5x the fastest autoregressive model listed here (1109 vs 201).
HumanEval pass@1 from the same table: the speed does not come with a large quality drop at this tier, though frontier models score higher on harder benchmarks like LiveCodeBench.

blocks.md: **Block diffusion** (BD3-LM, Arriola et al., 2025) makes the semi-autoregressive idea part of training. The sequence is split into blocks of size $L'$; the model is autoregressive across blocks and runs discrete diffusion within each block, using a block-causal attention mask. Earlier blocks are final, so their keys and values can be cached exactly, and the model can keep producing blocks for variable-length output.

scenes.caption: Three blocks of 4 tokens. Only block 1 is being generated; later blocks do not exist yet in BD3-LM (LLaDA's variant fills a fixed-length canvas instead).
Inside block 1, ordinary masked diffusion: some positions are committed after the first step, others stay masked.
Block 1 is finished and frozen. Its keys and values go into an exact KV cache, just as in a GPT.
Block 2 diffuses while attending to the cached block 1. Parallelism inside the block, autoregression between blocks.
All three blocks done. Block size 1 recovers an autoregressive model; block size equal to the whole sequence recovers plain masked diffusion.

blocks.md: Smaller blocks trade parallelism for likelihood. On LM1B after 65B training tokens, BD3-LM's perplexity bound improves from 30.60 at $L'=16$ to 29.83 at 8 and 28.23 at 4, against 31.78 for MDLM and 22.83 for an autoregressive Transformer. The authors also identify the high variance of the diffusion loss as a cause of the gap and reduce it with clipped noise schedules that avoid extreme mask rates.

**Open limitations.**
- The response length must be chosen before sampling (LLaDA reports low sensitivity, but it is still a fixed canvas).
- No exact KV cache for full bidirectional models; caching is approximate or needs block structure.
- Quality drops as more interdependent tokens are committed per step.
- Likelihood still lags: a scaling-law study by Nie et al. estimated masked diffusion needs about 16 times the compute of an autoregressive model for the same likelihood, though downstream tasks can tell a different story.
- Post-training such as reinforcement learning is less mature than for autoregressive models.

Diffusion LMs fit latency-sensitive, decode-heavy work where output can be refined globally: code completion and infilling (Mercury leads its fill-in-the-middle table), editing, and tasks that need context from both sides. For maximum quality per training FLOP or long free-form generation, autoregressive models remain the default.

blocks.question: A team needs exact KV caching and variable-length outputs but wants some parallel decoding. Which design fits best?
options: Pure masked diffusion over a fixed 1024-token canvas
BERT with a 15% masking ratio
An autoregressive model sampled at high temperature
Block diffusion with a small block size, autoregressive across blocks
blocks.explain: Block diffusion freezes finished blocks, so their keys and values are cached exactly and generation can continue block after block. Diffusion inside each block still commits several tokens per pass. A fixed canvas has neither property, and BERT cannot sample text.

blocks.question: LLaDA 8B Instruct beats GPT-4o on reversal poem completion but loses badly on forward completion. What is the best reading?
options: Training to predict tokens from both sides removes the directional bias, while GPT-4o's much larger training gives it a big edge in the direction it was trained on
LLaDA is a stronger model overall
The benchmark is broken because the scores do not add to 100
GPT-4o was evaluated with a causal mask removed
blocks.explain: LLaDA's forward and reversal scores are close (51.8 vs 45.6) because its objective covers all conditioning directions. GPT-4o is far stronger in the forward direction (82.7) but falls to 34.3 in reverse, the reversal curse. Neither result says LLaDA is better overall.
